    "explanation": "`_chmod_dangerous` calls `chmod_dash_mode` with the default `anywhere=False`. That means a dash mode placed after the first operand is never checked. Only the first operand is treated as the mode. The comment calls this \"the stricter of the two readings\", but it only covers the case where the first operand is the dangerous one. GNU chmod (which shell_writes.py's own docstring says reads a later dash mode as the mode) takes the trailing argument as the mode and treats every operand, including the numeric one, as a file. Example: `chmod 644 /usr/local/bin/x -w+s` is checked as mode 644, which is harmless, so nothing is denied. GNU chmod actually applies `-w+s`, which sets setuid/setgid on /usr/local/bin/x. Likewise, `chmod 644 /etc -o+w` makes /etc world-writable, while the rule sees only `644` and `_chmod_world_single` sees only `words[0]=644`. The config guard (shell_writes) already uses `anywhere=True` for this exact reason, but the danger rule does not.",
    "fix": "Check both readings. Compute `gnu_mode = chmod_dash_mode(args, anywhere=True)` and deny if either `words[0]` (the BSD reading) or `gnu_mode` (the GNU reading, with every operand as a target) is setuid or world-writable. Apply the same check in `_chmod_world_single`.",

    "confidence": 0.75,
    "_diff_anchor": "in_diff"

    "vulnerableCode": "for arg in args:\n    if arg == \"--\":\n        return None\n    if _CHMOD_DASH_MODE.fullmatch(arg):\n        return arg",
    "explanation": "`chmod_dash_mode` returns only the first dash-mode argument. GNU chmod joins every dash-mode argument into one comma-separated mode (`-x -w+s` becomes `-x,-w+s`; see the GNU chmod source for case 'r'..'7'). So `chmod -x -w+s /usr/local/bin/x` is judged by `_setuid(\"-x\")`, which is False, and the command is allowed. GNU chmod still applies `+s` and makes the file setuid. The same trick hides `-o+w` behind a harmless first dash mode on a broad target, e.g. `chmod -x -o+w /etc`.",
    "fix": "Collect every argument that matches `_CHMOD_DASH_MODE` (up to `--`), join them with ',' and return the combined mode. Alternatively, evaluate `_setuid`/`_world_writable` on each one.",
